appraisal_events.evidence: Old acquaintances from Combray reduce the marriage to 'c'est tout simplement Mlle Swann,' mock how many men her mother has 'held onto,' and note that the wedding witness, 'le «Baron» de Charlus,' was 'ce vieux qui entretenait déjà la mère autrefois au vu et au su de Swann.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Provincial gossip deflates Gilberte's new grandeur as marquise de Saint-Loup by tying her back to her mother Odette's disreputable history as a kept woman, and in the same breath exposes Charlus, the wedding witness, as one of that history's participants.

appraisal_events.evidence: Adopted by Charlus into a name 'qui était dans la famille des Guermantes,' the tailor's niece marries into the Cambremer line; the mother calls it 'la récompense de la vertu... un mariage à la fin d'un roman de Mme Sand,' which the narrator privately counters as 'le prix du vice... un roman de Balzac.' Meanwhile the bridegroom's mother, 'méchante de nature,' privately complains the bride 'sortait on ne savait d'où' and 'avait des dents si mal rangées.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The niece's ascent from 'petite nièce d'un giletier' into a near-royal adopted name and an aristocratic marriage is a real, marked elevation, sentimentally endorsed by the mother's fairy-tale framing; but the narrator's private ironizing rejoinder and the future mother-in-law's spiteful private disparagement both qualify that elevation without overturning it.

status_effects.explanation: Gossip publicly reasserts her mother's scandalous reputation and casts doubt on the propriety of her origins and her wedding party, undercutting the marriage's outward brilliance even as it formally makes her a marquise.
His role as wedding witness becomes the occasion for gossip to expose him as Odette's former keeper, discrediting him in the same stroke as the bride.

She visibly crosses from being 'la petite nièce d'un giletier' into the aristocratic Guermantes-adjacent clan the Cambremers 'n'espéraient pas pouvoir jamais planter leur tente,' via Charlus's adoption and a titled marriage.
Her future mother-in-law privately disparages her uncertain origins and appearance, a distinct qualifying note against the otherwise celebratory framing of the match.
The narrator explicitly frames her as 'méchante de nature,' preferring to humiliate her own family over taking pride in the brilliant alliance, a direct authorial diminishment of her character.

ambiguities: The gossip passage's reference to 'le mari, qui naturellement n'est pas noble' and 'un Monsieur Dupont ou Durand quelconque' is confusingly worded and may conflate details of the Saint-Loup/Gilberte and Cambremer/d'Oloron marriages rather than cleanly describing one groom; it is treated here as part of the general discrediting gossip around Gilberte's marriage without resolving exactly whom it targets.
